title: Binary relation
parts: is a set of some (possibly all) of the
ordered pairs of elements of S.
note: A binary relation on S can be represented as pairs or as directed edges.
wrong: R must include every possible ordered pair.
R contains only individual elements of S.
R is a number equal to the size of S squared.

title: Membership in a relation
example: If R is “less than”, then (2,5) ∈ R because 2 < 5.
note: Order matters: (5,2) need not belong to the same relation.
wrong: The pair (y,x) must also belong to R.
x equals y.
Neither x nor y can be related.

title: Factorial
parts: Multiply all the positive integers from 1 through n.
note: For non-negative integers, n! counts the orderings of n distinct objects. The empty product gives 0! = 1.
wrong: Multiply n by itself n times.
Add all integers from 1 through n.
Multiply n by 2.

title: Graph, vertices and edges
parts: consists of a set of vertices V
and a set of edges E.
example: V = {a,b,c}, E = {{a,b}, {b,c}} describes an undirected path.
note: Directed edges are ordered pairs. Undirected edges can be written as two-element sets.
wrong: G is the product of V and E.
V is the edge set and E is the vertex set.
G has exactly two vertices.

title: Vertex degree
parts: The degree of vertex v, counting each incident end of an edge.
example: If a is connected to b, c and d in a simple undirected graph, deg(a) = 3.
note: In directed graphs distinguish in-degree from out-degree. An undirected loop counts twice.
wrong: The distance from v to every vertex.
The total number of vertices in the graph.
The discovery time of v in DFS.

title: Shortest path distance
parts: The length of a shortest path
example: In an unweighted graph, the path s → a → v has length 2.
note: BFS finds these distances in unweighted graphs. Unreachable vertices are often assigned ∞.
wrong: The length of the longest path from s to v.
The number of all possible paths from s to v.
The number of neighbours of v.

title: Graph eccentricity
parts: is the greatest, over all vertices u in V, of
the shortest-path distance from v to u.
example: If BFS distances from v are 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, then ecc(v) = 3.
note: Take shortest-path distances first, then choose the largest. A distance to an unreachable vertex may be ∞.
wrong: The smallest distance from v to any vertex.
The sum of the distances from v.
The number of edges touching v.

title: Depth-first search timestamps
example: u starts at time 1, v starts at 2, v finishes at 5, u finishes at 8.
note: These nested intervals mean v is a descendant of u in the DFS forest.
wrong: v finishes after u finishes.
u and v are in disjoint DFS subtrees.
v is discovered before u.

title: Big O upper bound
parts: of a constant multiple of n squared.
example: 3n² + 10n + 5 is O(n²). A linear function is also O(n²).
note: Big-O is an upper bound, not necessarily an exact growth rate or a synonym for worst case.
wrong: The running time is exactly n squared for every n.
The running time has a lower bound of n squared.
The running time must grow strictly faster than n squared.

title: Big theta tight bound
parts: is bounded above and below by positive constant multiples
of n, for sufficiently large n.
note: Theta is a tight asymptotic bound.
wrong: T(n) is exactly n for every n.
T(n) has only an upper bound proportional to n.
T(n) must be quadratic.

title: Big omega lower bound
parts: of a positive constant multiple of n.
note: Omega describes a lower bound; it does not automatically mean best case.
wrong: T(n) has an upper bound proportional to n.
T(n) is always exactly n.
T(n) grows more slowly than every linear function.

title: Little o
parts: grows strictly more slowly, asymptotically, than
example: n ∈ o(n²) because n/n² → 0 as n grows.
note: Little-o is stricter than Big-O. n is O(n), but not o(n).
wrong: f and g have exactly the same asymptotic order.
f grows strictly faster than g.
f is equal to g for every n.

title: Linear time on a graph
parts: An asymptotic upper bound proportional to
example: BFS with adjacency lists runs in O(|V| + |E|).
note: The vertical bars count elements. This bound depends on the representation and algorithm.
wrong: The number of vertices multiplied by the number of edges.
The number of vertices squared.
The exact time in seconds of BFS.

title: A* evaluation function
parts: The A* evaluation score for node n
is the cost already paid to reach n
plus the estimated remaining cost to a goal.
example: If g(n) = 7 and h(n) = 4, then f(n) = 11.
note: Here n is a search node, not the input size used in Big-O.
wrong: The cost to reach n minus the remaining estimate.
Only the estimated remaining cost.
Only the cost already paid.

title: Admissible heuristic
parts: The estimated remaining cost from n
example: A heuristic of 4 is admissible when the true remaining cost is 6.
note: h* uses a star to denote the true optimal cost here. This is the admissibility condition.
wrong: The heuristic always overestimates the true remaining cost.
The heuristic must equal the true cost.
The heuristic is the cost already paid.

title: Branching factor and depth
parts: An asymptotic upper bound proportional to
raised to the solution depth d.
example: With branching factor 3 and depth 4, bᵈ = 81.
note: This is a common search-tree bound; exact bounds depend on when goals are tested and nodes are generated.
wrong: The branching factor multiplied by the depth.
The depth raised to the branching factor.
The branching factor plus the depth.

title: Kleene star
parts: the set of all finite strings over the alphabet Σ, including the empty string.
example: If Σ = {0,1}, then ε, 0, 10 and 110 belong to Σ*.
note: The star is Kleene star here. It does not mean multiplication or an optimal cost.
wrong: w is exactly one symbol of Σ.
w must be an infinite string.
w must contain every symbol of Σ exactly once.

title: Language accepted by a machine
parts: The language consisting of all strings accepted by machine M.
example: If M accepts exactly the binary strings ending in 1, then 01 ∈ L(M).
note: For a Turing machine, strings outside L(M) may be rejected or may run forever.
wrong: All strings on which M halts, including rejected strings.
The number of states in M.
The set of strings M rejects.

title: DFA transition
parts: given current state q and input symbol a
example: In a DFA, reading a in state q moves the machine to state r.
note: This notation is for a DFA. An NFA transition can return a set of states.
wrong: q is the input symbol and a is the next state.
Every state moves to r without reading input.
The machine accepts all strings ending in r.
